lead: A mass on a spring with a damper obeys the same second-order equation as an inductor, resistor and capacitor in series. So a mechanical system can be redrawn as an electrical circuit, and circuit tools — impedance, mesh analysis, simulation — then give the same transfer function. Two standard mappings exist: force–voltage and force–current. Engineers use them to test a vehicle suspension or a MEMS accelerometer in a circuit simulator, and examiners use them to check whether you see the equation behind the hardware.
prereq: You need: 1.4 for masses, springs and dampers, and 1.3 for the transfer function.

sections.h3: Why a circuit can stand in for a machine

blocks.text: Write Newton's second law for one mass m (kg) pulled by a force F(t) against a spring k (N/m) and a viscous damper b (N·s/m). The displacement is x (m). Then write Kirchhoff's voltage law for an inductor L (H), a resistor R (Ω) and a capacitor C (F) in series, driven by a voltage v(t), with charge q (C).
m ẍ + b ẋ + k x = F(t)   and   L q̈ + R q̇ + (1/C) q = v(t)
blocks.where: ẍ is d²x/dt² (m/s²), ẋ is dx/dt (m/s); q̇ is current i (A), q̈ is di/dt (A/s); L, R, C are inductance, resistance, capacitance.

blocks.text: The two equations have identical shape. Match term by term and the force–voltage (F–V) analogy falls out. It is also called the direct or impedance analogy.
Read the last row twice. The spring becomes the reciprocal of capacitance, so a stiff spring (large k) is a small capacitor. Most marks are lost exactly here.

sections.h3: The force–current analogy and how to build the circuit

blocks.text: The second mapping makes force the current instead of the voltage. It is called the force–current (F–I), inverse or mobility analogy. It exists because in a multi-mass mechanical system the same force passes through elements joined end to end, while velocity is shared only at a common junction. Making force the current lets those elements sit in series, as they do physically.

items: Draw each mass separately and mark every force on it: applied force, spring force, damper force.
Write the force balance for each mass, then compare it with the L–R–C equation to confirm the mapping.
Replace each element by its electrical partner from the chosen table, keeping the numbers unchanged.
Connect by the sharing rule: in F–V, elements with the same velocity go in series (same current); elements carrying the same force go in parallel (same voltage).
Add the applied force as the source, then write the circuit equation and check it matches the mechanical one.

blocks.text: For a single mass on a wall, the mass, spring and damper all move at the same velocity, so all three are in series — exactly the L–R–C loop. The force F becomes a voltage source of value F volts in that loop.

sections.h3: Reading results back, and where the analogy is used

blocks.text: Once the circuit exists, every mechanical number has a circuit twin. The natural frequency and damping ratio are the same formulas written in two languages.

blocks.where: ωn is the undamped natural frequency (rad/s), ζ is the damping ratio (no unit), and the right-hand forms use the analogous L, R, C.

items: Check both sides give the same ωn and ζ before trusting the mapping.
A circuit simulator then shows the step response without building the machine — used for vehicle suspensions, machine-tool mounts and MEMS sensors.
Only linear elements carry over. Coulomb friction and backlash do not have a resistor or capacitor twin, so the analogy stops there.

figure.caption: Each mechanical value maps to one electrical value under the force–voltage analogy: mass 2 kg to 2 H, damper 3 N·s/m to 3 Ω, spring 4 N/m to 0.25 F.

spec.aria: Three mechanical elements m = 2, b = 3 and k = 4 map by the force-voltage analogy to L = 2 H, R = 3 Ω and C = 0.25 F.

examples.question: A translational system has m = 2 kg, b = 3 N·s/m and k = 4 N/m. Using the force–voltage analogy, find the equivalent inductance, resistance and capacitance. Also confirm the natural frequency and damping ratio of the circuit match the mechanical system.
steps: Force balance: m ẍ + b ẋ + k x = F(t), with m = 2 kg, b = 3 N·s/m, k = 4 N/m.
Series RLC equation: L q̈ + R q̇ + q/C = v(t). Matching terms gives L = m, R = b, 1/C = k.
Mechanical ωn = √(k/m) = √(4/2) = √2 = 1.4142 rad/s. Circuit ωn = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(2 × 0.25) = 1/√0.5 = 1.4142 rad/s. They agree.
examples.answer: The equivalent circuit is L = 2 H, R = 3 Ω and C = 0.25 F in series with a voltage source v = F, and it has ωn = 1.4142 rad/s and ζ = 0.5303, the same as the mechanical system.
examples.check:
m = 2.0
b = 3.0
k = 4.0
L = m
R = b
C = 1.0 / k
wn_mech = (k / m) ** 0.5
wn_elec = 1.0 / (L * C) ** 0.5
zeta_mech = b / (2.0 * (k * m) ** 0.5)
zeta_elec = (R / 2.0) * (C / L) ** 0.5
print(L)
print(R)
print(C)
print(round(wn_mech, 4))
print(round(zeta_mech, 4))
print(round(wn_elec, 4))
print(round(zeta_elec, 4))

traps: In the force–voltage analogy the spring maps to 1/C, so k = 4 N/m gives C = 0.25 F, never C = 4 F.
In the force–current analogy the damper maps to conductance G = 1/R, so b = 3 N·s/m is G = 3 S, which is R = 0.333 Ω.
Mass is inductance only in the F–V analogy; in F–I the mass becomes a capacitance. Writing L = m in both is the commonest single error.
Do not mix the two analogies in one circuit. Pick one table and use it for every element and for the source.
Velocity maps to current, not to voltage, under F–V. Swapping them reverses the series/parallel rule and the circuit equation no longer matches.

quiz.q: State the three element pairs of the force–voltage analogy for mass, damper and spring.
quiz.a: Mass → inductance L, damper → resistance R, spring → elastance 1/C (so the capacitance is 1/k).

quiz.q: Why does an electrical circuit give the same transfer function as a mechanical system?
quiz.a: The mechanical force balance m ẍ + b ẋ + k x = F and the series RLC equation L q̈ + R q̇ + q/C = v are the same linear second-order equation. Terms that occupy the same place in the equation must behave identically, so the transfer function, ωn and ζ are unchanged.

quiz.q: A system has m = 5 kg, b = 2 N·s/m and k = 20 N/m. Find the F–V equivalent elements and the damping ratio.
Under the force–current analogy, a damper has b = 0.5 N·s/m. Find its conductance and resistance.
quiz.a: Conductance G = b = 0.5 S. Resistance R = 1/G = 1/0.5 = 2 Ω.

quiz.q: A student writes C = k = 4 F for a spring of stiffness 4 N/m and still gets a correct-looking answer. What error appears in the natural frequency?
quiz.a: The correct value is C = 1/k = 0.25 F. With C = 4 F the circuit gives ωn = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(2 × 4) = 0.3536 rad/s, while the true value is 1.4142 rad/s — wrong by a factor of 4, which is √(k²).

quiz.q: Two masses are joined by a spring. Which analogy makes the circuit easier to draw, and why?
quiz.a: The force–current analogy. The spring carries the same force as each mass connection, and force maps to current, so those elements sit in series in one loop, matching the physical chain. In the F–V analogy the shared force would need a parallel connection across a common node, which is harder to draw without error.

quiz.q: Name one class of mechanical behaviour the analogy cannot represent, and say why.
quiz.a: Nonlinear effects such as Coulomb friction, backlash or a hardening spring. Linear inductance, resistance and capacitance cannot reproduce them, so the analogy holds only for linear elements.

beyond: Not for the exam. The two analogies are special cases of a wider modelling method called bond graphs, which track power flow instead of matching equations term by term. Textbooks also call the force–voltage mapping the impedance analogy and the force–current mapping the mobility analogy, and those two names will find better search results. Modern controller design often skips the hand-drawn circuit and builds a Simulink or SPICE model directly from the mechanical equation, but the mapping is how those tools cross between domains. Circuit simulators are still used to prototype MEMS accelerometers and loudspeaker suspensions before any hardware is built.
